task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: sample size power for series-level analysis
confounding by team strength in adherence-win relationship
lookahead bias in deriving recommended mix
defining and quantifying adherence to a probabilistic mix

historical_evidence.finding: Avg |delta| on leverage buckets 4.5pp to 24.0pp; 4 of 8 sides best matched opener #3, not rank-1; single-game horizon; no outcome comparison.
Higher AVOID share predicts losing: game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 but team-quality confound; series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 with n=50, underpowered; low AVOID-share bin 52.6% win vs 25-50% bin 37.0%.
Eq vs actual +1.16 pts/100; beats actual 127/240 (53%); equilibrium PPP is model-implied not observed.
Raw gap aligned-deviated +5.18 ORtg; strength-controlled gap +3.27 ORtg; model regret median +25.94 ORtg.

failed_approaches.what_failed: single-game measurement of execution conformance to recommended mix (descriptive)
failed_approaches.why: no outcome link; high variance; unclear failure mechanism

failed_approaches.what_failed: series-level AVOID share vs winning analysis
failed_approaches.why: sample too small (n=50); team-quality confounding; underpowered (~80 series needed)

failed_approaches.what_failed: adversarial equilibrium recommendation vs actual offense
failed_approaches.why: equilibrium PPP model-implied, not observed; marginal result (53% beat rate)

evidence_establishes: Alignment with a model-recommended play-type mix (offensive) improves points per possession in holdout games when controlling for team strength (SF-[prior work]).
Series-level analysis of a specific defensive mix recommendation (AVOID share) was underpowered and confounded by team quality, requiring ~80 series for p<0.05 (SF-[prior work]).
Single-game descriptive measures of mix conformance show large gaps and no direct outcome link (SF-[prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix at the series level predicts winning after controlling for team quality and other confounders.
What the precise operational definition of 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' is, and whether it can be derived without lookahead bias from available data.
That a suppression-conditional mix adherence measure has sufficient reliability and variation to support a series-level test.
That any observed association would be causal rather than reflecting underlying defensive talent or opponent adjustments.
own_inferences: The combination of low statistical power (n=54 series) and confounding by team strength makes a clean series-level test infeasible with current data.
Even if a suppression-conditional recommended mix could be derived from historical data, the adherence measure would be model-dependent, noisy, and vulnerable to overfitting.
Expanding to game-level outcomes could improve power, but would change the estimand away from the stated 'predicts winning' and still faces team-quality confounding.
Without 6-8 seasons of data to reach ~100 series, a series-level binary-outcome analysis is unlikely to yield definitive results.
uncertainties: The exact definition of 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' is not specified; it could refer to defensive scheme (e.g., drop, blitz, switch) conditional on ball-handler suppression state, but classification from play-by-play may be unreliable.
Whether derived play-type possession records include defensive play types (e.g., coverage type, tagger help) or only offensive actions.
The degree of measurement error in assigning defensive schemes from the available data.
Whether regular-season team strength fully accounts for talent confounding, or whether playoff-specific factors (injuries, tactical adjustments) add unmeasured confounds.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved evidence (SF-[prior work]) directly demonstrates that a similar series-level defensive-mix hypothesis was underpowered and confounded, requiring around 80 series to reach significance; with only 54 series available, the same risks apply, making a naive proceed decision inadvisable. SF-[prior work] further shows that observed mix conformance can be noisy even at the single-game level. The combined record shifts the assessment from 'maybe' to 'not testable as posed with current data'.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 54 playoff series are available, whereas a similar design (SF-[prior work]) required ~80 series for p<0.05; a noisier suppression-conditional adherence measure would need an even larger sample.

Good teams tend both to execute recommended defensive strategies and to win; without strong controls (e.g., regular-season net rating, opponent strength, prior playoff performance), any adherence-win correlation is confounded.
Classifying every defensive possession into a suppression-conditional scheme from play-by-play and matchup data is error-prone, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio of the adherence metric.
Some recommended strategies may appear only sporadically; a floor effect could compress the adherence measure, limiting its predictive value.
If the recommended mix is derived from the same season’s outcomes or uses information from later in the series, it may induce a spurious association with winning.

prior_work.summary: SF-[prior work] addressed a closely related hypothesis (AVOID share vs series win) and found it untestable due to small sample and confounding. SF-[prior work] showed that offensive mix alignment correlates with offensive efficiency in holdout games, but not at the series level. SF-[prior work] described poor single-game mix conformance without an outcome link. Together they partially cover the measurement and design challenges, but the specific suppression-conditional defensive mix hypothesis remains untested and likely untestable with current data.

risks.text: n=54 series; estimated need ~100 series for adequate power given noisy adherence measures and binary outcome.
Team quality is a plausible confounder; differences in defensive talent and coaching discipline could drive both adherence and winning.
Suppression-conditional defensive scheme classification may have low inter-rater reliability from play-by-play alone.
Defining 'recommended' from within-series or within-season data risks using future information to predict past winning.
The suppression-conditional mix may rarely be executed, so adherence metrics could be sparse and volatile at the series level.

design.estimand: The causal effect of a team’s series-average adherence to a pre-specified suppression-conditional defensive mix on the probability of winning the playoff series, holding constant pre-playoffs team strength.
design.sample: All playoff series from 2022-23 through 2025-26 for which complete play-by-play and defensive matchup data are available (54 series).
design.power: Estimated power for a medium effect size (OR ≈ 2) at α = 0.05 is ~30–40%; minimum detectable effect size far exceeds what is plausible, making the test underpowered.
design.controls: Regular-season net rating for each team, opponent net rating, home-court advantage, and possibly prior playoff performance. Residualizing within team-season may be attempted but would further reduce degrees of freedom.
design.falsification: Shuffle adherence assignments across series (preserving team pairing) and verify that the estimated effect disappears; also replace the recommended mix with a randomly generated mix to rule out spurious correlation.
design.multiplicity: Only one primary adherence metric tested; sensitivity checks using alternative mix definitions to be noted but not used for inference.
design.decision_rule: p < 0.05 (two-sided) on the coefficient of adherence in a logistic regression of series win, after including team strength controls, with pre-registered model specification.
design.data_version: Data snapshot as of 2026-06-16, based on NBA stats API play-by-play and derived play-type possession records from the project graph database.
